newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese nuclear power plants put up oil fences.
newsitem.headline: Japanese nuclear power plants put up oil fences.

text.p: Japanese nuclear power plants on Friday erected sea fences to keep out oil slicks in a new danger posed by a spill from an ageing Russian tanker.

As one of the worst oil spills in Japan's history spread across a widening swathe of coastline, Tokyo officials called on Moscow to find out how the accident happened and detail what it would do to help.

A Maritime Safety Agency (MSA) spokesman said that eight days after the accident, 73 oil slicks had either washed ashore or were heading for a 450-km (285-mile) stretch of coast on the Sea of Japan, about 320 kms (200 miles) west of Tokyo.
Transport Minister Makoto Koga, who heads a disaster task force, said the cleanup effort was running into problems.
"Cleanup efforts are getting more difficult because the oil keeps on spreading over a wide area. We're running out of ways to clean up," he told a news conference during a visit to the area.
The latest threat was to 15 reactors, the biggest concentration of nuclear power plants in the world, which rely on seawater to cool their systems and avoid a meltdown.
The plants include Monju, the world's second-largest fast-breeder reactor. Fast-breeder reactors produce more plutonium than they consume.
Japan, which already relies on nuclear plants for nearly one-third of its power, regards them as a pillar of its energy policy into the 21st century.
The MSA spokesman said several slicks, about 10 to 15 km (six to 10 miles) offshore, were heading for the plants and if they kept their direction could threaten the plants by Sunday.
The biggest slick was six km (3.7 miles) long and 100 metres (yards) wide. Another slick had already come ashore about 20 km (12 miles) from the nearest reactor.
Plant operators said operations would not be affected if the oil stayed near the surface because intake pipes are set about five metres (16 feet) below sea level.
A spokesman for Kansai Electric Power Co, which operates 11 reactors around Wakasa Bay, said the reactors were operating as usual and they had no plans yet to lower power production.

"We have set up oil fences and the pipe pulling in water is four to seven metres below the sea surface. If the oil enters the coolant pipes, it could lower the cooling effect," a spokesman told Reuters.
Monju's operators, Power Reactor Nuclear Fuel Development Corporation, said they also had erected 200-metre (yard) long fences to keep oil away from its intake pipes.
Authorities still do not know the extent of the leakage from the 13,157-tonne tanker Nakhodka, built 26 years ago, which was carrying 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of fuel oil.
They initially estimated 3,700 tonnes (26,000 barrels) of oil spilled but now believe this figure is far too low.
The 31-man crew on the tanker, which broke in two, were rescued but the captain is missing and presumed dead.
The bow of the tanker has washed up on rocks in Mikuni, a fishing town of 20,000 people devastated by the spill.
The stern, where two-thirds of the oil was stored, sank about 115 km (70 miles) offshore and much of the oil now leaking from there has not yet even reached shore.
The shoreline threatened by the spill spans six prefectures on the Sea of Japan, stretching from around Kyoto to the Noto Peninsula, the Fisheries Agency said in a statement.
The area includes some of Japan's most fertile fishing areas as well as small ports and tourist resorts.
